Use this page to build your study population, once you know which registers
your study needs and before you extract any covariates. You decide who could
have entered the study at all (the source population), find the exposed people
or cases, give each of them an index date, and exclude those who already had the
outcome. When you are done you have a cohort: a table with `pnr` and
`index_date` per person, which every later phase builds on ([Phase
11](extract-variables.qmd) to [Phase 13](analysis.qmd)).

Finding exposed people or cases in hospital data uses the LPR (the National Patient Register) extraction pattern
from [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd), so read that page first. What you
do after this page depends on your study design, see [the end of this
page](#what-now-choose-your-design).

<details>
<summary>What is an index date?</summary>

**Index date** is the point in time that marks the start of follow-up for a given person.

- **Exposed:** the date the person received the exposure (e.g. surgery date, diagnosis date, first prescription dispensed)
- **Comparator cohort:** the index date assigned from the matched exposed person

Everything that follows - outcome date, covariates at baseline, follow-up time - is calculated relative to index date. The definition of index date is crucial for study validity.

</details>

::: {.callout-warning title="Structural guidance, not verified code"}
The examples show the shape of each step. They have **not yet been run end to end
on real register data**, so treat them as a starting point: check the column names
against your own delivery, and check the logic against your analysis plan.
:::

## Step 1 - Define the source population {#step-1 .step-heading}

Before you look for the exposed, decide who could have entered the study at
all. That is the source population, and two things decide it: your data
delivery and a residence criterion.

::: {.callout-important}
**Your data delivery sets the outer limit.** DST (Statistics Denmark) only delivers data on the
population your project is approved for. If your delivery is "persons in BEF
2005-2024", then a person who only lived in Denmark in 2003 does not exist in
your extract at all - and no code can pull them in. Check your project guide
first. The registers below can make the timing of residence precise within
your delivery, but they cannot add people to it.
:::

### BEF alone cannot decide residence

BEF (the population register) is a snapshot: DST delivers it as quarterly
pictures, each a status on the last day of the quarter ([Nyt fra
Forskningsservice
4/2019](https://dst.dk/ext/2940168985/0/forskning/Ekstra-Nyt-fra-Forskningsservice-4-kvartal-2019--pdf),
PDF, Danish). Check which reference dates your own delivery has.
That means BEF gets it wrong in both directions:

- **Too many included:** the person is in that year's snapshot, but had
  emigrated or died by your index date.
- **Too few included:** the person is *not* in that year's snapshot, but was
  genuinely resident on the index date. That happens if they had emigrated at
  the time of the snapshot and moved home later the same year.

You can filter your way out of the first error, but not out of the second: a
filter can only remove people from the pool BEF already found, never add the
ones missing from it. So residence has to be decided on
events, not on snapshots.

### Use BEF and VNDS together

You need both registers, plus the death register:

- **BEF:** the population and demographics: who exists, date of birth and sex.
  Use all snapshots in your study window combined (the union), not one year at a
  time.
- **VNDS (migrations):** the events: immigrations and emigrations with dates.
  VNDS holds only migration events, so a person born in Denmark who never left
  has no rows in VNDS. Absence of events is the normal case, not an error.
- **DOD (deaths):** the date of death, applied on top.

The rule is therefore a default with exceptions: resident since birth, unless
VNDS says otherwise. For each person, find the latest VNDS event before the
index date:

  | Latest event before index | Resident at index? | Residence period starts |
  | ------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------- |
  | `"I"` (immigration)       | Yes                | the event date          |
  | `"U"` (emigration)        | No                 | -                       |
  | no events                 | Yes                | the date of birth       |

That start date is what you measure a continuous residence requirement from
(e.g. "at least 5 years in Denmark before index"). It is not the same as the
earliest year the person appears in BEF: someone seen in BEF in 2005, but living
abroad 2006-2012 and moving home in 2013, has only two years of continuous
residence at an index date in 2015.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Check these six things before you trust the rule.**

- **The event codes:** run `count(indud_kode)` on your own VNDS. The guide uses
  `"I"` and `"U"`, but confirm the values in your delivery.
- **Immigration before 1971:** CPR (the Civil Registration System) only has complete immigration and emigration
  data from 1971 (see [Further information](#further-information)). A person
  born abroad who immigrated before that has no events, and the rule above
  wrongly counts them as resident since birth.
- **Greenland:** a status of its own in CPR, not the same as emigration. Find
  out how moves there appear in your delivery.
- **Disappeared people:** people whose address is unknown to the authorities
  leave the population without an emigration event in VNDS, because DST counts them
  separately from emigrations ([DST's documentation of the population
  figures](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/statistikdokumentation/befolkningen)),
  so the rule above counts them as resident; they drop out of BEF, which is
  one more reason to require presence in BEF as well.
- **Short stays abroad:** decide whether a short gap breaks "continuous"
  residence, and write the choice down in your methods.
- **Register coverage is not residence:** five years of residence only gives you
  five years of lookback if the registers cover those five years too.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Another way: residence from the CPR address history"}
Municipality codes can also be used to assess residence in Denmark. CPR
keeps a running residence history: one period per address, with municipality
code and dates. With it you can look residence up directly (was there a period
spanning the index date?) instead of deriving it from BEF snapshots and VNDS
events. CPR has complete information on municipality of residence in Denmark
from 1971 and full address from 1977; Greenland is a separate series
from May 1972. The residence history says nothing about whether the person is
alive, so the date of death still has to be fetched separately. See [Further
information](#further-information) for the source.

Do not read the gaps uncritically. A gap in the residence history can be either a genuine stay abroad or a missing
registration, and the history alone cannot tell you which. Count how many
people in your own cohort have a gap before you decide how to treat them.
:::

### Code: the source population at study start

```r
# Step 1: the source population at study start (BEF + VNDS) --------------------
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(dplyr)   # the verbs are translated to SQL and run in DuckDB

# Here residence is decided at ONE fixed date: study start. That is the simplest
# version, and it gives a list at person level. If each person has their own index
# date the rule is the same - but the date only exists later, see the note below
# the code.
STUDY_START <- as.Date("2010-01-01")   # we choose: first day of the study

# 1.1 The population and date of birth (BEF, all snapshots combined) -----------
# distinct() gives one row per person across ALL years in the window. Using a
# single year's snapshot loses those who moved home later that year.
bef <- read_register("bef") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  distinct(pnr, foed_dag, koen)

# 1.2 Latest migration event BEFORE study start --------------------------------
# Everything is lazy: DuckDB does the lookup, and we only fetch the result at the
# end. Pulling VNDS into R first fills memory for no reason.
vnds <- read_register("vnds") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  select(pnr, indud_kode, haend_dato)

latest_event <- vnds %>%
  filter(haend_dato <= STUDY_START) %>%                 # only events before study start
  group_by(pnr) %>%
  slice_max(haend_dato, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%   # the latest of them
  ungroup() %>%
  select(pnr, last_code = indud_kode, last_date = haend_dato)

# 1.3 Decide residence and apply the criteria ----------------------------------
# left_join: people WITHOUT events get NA - and NA here means "never left",
# i.e. resident since birth. That is the default, not an exception.
source_population <- bef %>%
  left_join(latest_event, by = "pnr") %>%
  mutate(
    resident       = is.na(last_code) | last_code == "I",   # no event OR last one was an entry
    resident_since = if_else(is.na(last_code), foed_dag, last_date)
  ) %>%
  filter(resident) %>%                                                 # resident at study start
  filter(as.numeric(STUDY_START - resident_since) / 365.25 >= 5) %>%   # 5 years continuous residence
  collect()   # only now is data pulled into RAM
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Does each person have their own index date?** Then the same rule applies,
but it has to be used where the date exists, not here. The index date is not a
property of the person:

- **The exposed** get their index date in Step 2 (the exposure date). Residence
  is therefore decided for them when you prepare the exposed on [Comparison
  cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd).
- **Comparison persons** are only assigned an index date at the match itself,
  and the *same* person can be a candidate at several different index dates -
  and be resident at one but not the other. So residence is decided per (person,
  index date) at match time on [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd), never
  once and for all.

So the source population here is at person level, while eligibility at index is
at the level of person and date.
:::

## Step 2 - Identify the exposed (or cases) {.step-heading}

You scan the register that defines your exposure. You do not have a
`cohort_pnrs` list yet, so you query the entire register and filter on the
exposure criterion. The exposure can be defined in several ways:

  | Type                             | Example                         | Register                                                   |
  | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Surgery / procedure (SKS code)   | Bariatric surgery KJDF10/KJDF11 | `lpr_sksopr` (LPR2), `lpr_a_procregistrering` (LPR3)        |
  | Hospital diagnosis (ICD code)    | Type 2 diabetes E11             | `lpr_diag` + `lpr_adm`, `lpr_a_diagnose` + `lpr_a_kontakt` |
  | Medication exposure (ATC code)   | Metformin A10BA02               | LMDB (the prescription register)                                                       |
  | Clinical measurement / biomarker | BMI (body mass index) > 35, HbA1c > 75 mmol/mol   | Laboratory results (HbA1c), clinical quality databases or project-specific data (BMI) |

Register names may vary on your project - see [Overview of
registers](register-reference.qmd).

The examples use `read_register()`; it requires fastreg set up with the path to
your registers - see [Parquet and fastreg](parquet-and-fastreg.qmd#convert-sas-to-parquet) if
you did not convert them from SAS (a statistics program) yourself.

<details>
<summary>Example A: exposure defined by a surgery or procedure (SKS codes)</summary>

`lpr_sksopr` holds the procedure code (`c_opr`) and `recnum`, but not `pnr` or date; those are in `lpr_adm`. So you join the two on `recnum` to get person, date and procedure together, the same pattern as for diagnoses, see [Understand LPR](understand-lpr.qmd#contact-and-diagnosis-tables).

```r
# Step 2A: identify the exposed via SKS codes ----------------------------------
library(fastreg) # read_register - read a register by name
library(dplyr)   # filter, select, group_by, slice, ungroup, bind_rows, mutate
# without fastreg: open_dataset("E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/<register>/") %>% rename_with(tolower) for each register

# Adapt these codes to your study
# Code texts from the SKS browser (medinfo.dk/sks/brows.php). Check the validity
# dates for your study period in SKS: KJDF40/KJDF41 are not in the 2005 edition of the
# SKS operation classification, so they cannot catch sleeve operations before
# they were introduced.
RYGB     <- c("KJDF10", "KJDF11") # "Gastric bypass", "Laparoskopisk gastric bypass"
SG       <- c("KJDF40", "KJDF41") # "Sleeve gastrektomi", "Laparoskopisk sleeve gastrektomi"
# KJDF96/KJDF97 are "Anden (laparoskopisk) volumenindskrænkende operation på
# mavesæk" (other volume-reducing stomach operation), not sleeve codes as such.
# Add them only if "other" belongs in your exposure definition.
BS_CODES <- c(RYGB, SG)           # combined vector

# 1A.1 LPR2: procedures 1996 to 31 March 2019 ----------------------------------
lpr_sksopr <- read_register("lpr_sksopr") %>%
  rename_with(tolower)
lpr_adm    <- read_register("lpr_adm") %>%
  rename_with(tolower)

exp_lpr2 <- lpr_sksopr %>%
  filter(c_opr %in% !!BS_CODES) %>%                        # only bariatric procedures
  select(recnum, sks_code = c_opr) %>%                      # recnum is the join key to lpr_adm
  inner_join(
    lpr_adm %>% select(pnr, recnum, index_date = d_inddto), # attach pnr and date
    by = "recnum"
  ) %>%
  collect()

# 1A.2 LPR3: procedures from 2019 onwards --------------------------------------
proc <- read_register("lpr_a_procregistrering") %>%
  rename_with(tolower)
lpr_a_k  <- read_register("lpr_a_kontakt") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  filter(lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3")                  # only genuine LPR3 contacts, see Understand LPR

exp_lpr3 <- proc %>%
  filter(proc_kode %in% !!BS_CODES) %>%                     # only bariatric procedures
  select(dw_ek_kontakt, sks_code = proc_kode) %>%           # dw_ek_kontakt joins to the contact
  inner_join(
    lpr_a_k %>% select(pnr, dw_ek_kontakt, index_date = kont_starttidspunkt),
    by = "dw_ek_kontakt"
  ) %>%
  collect() %>%
  mutate(index_date = as.Date(index_date))                  # datetime → date

# 1A.3 Combine and take one procedure per person (the first) -------------------
# The result is called "exposed" - only the exposed group, NOT the full cohort yet
exposed <- bind_rows(exp_lpr2, exp_lpr3) %>%
  group_by(pnr) %>%                                        # group per person
  arrange(index_date) %>%                                   # oldest date first
  slice(1) %>%                                              # one procedure per person (the first)
  ungroup() %>%                                             # release grouping (see Phase 12)
  mutate(exposed = 1L)                                      # mark as exposed (1 = yes)

nrow(exposed)                                              # number of unique operated individuals
```

Note that `exposed` holds only the operated individuals. The full cohort
(exposed + comparison group) is built on [Comparison
cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd) and saved as `cohort` - and it is `cohort`, not
`exposed`, that the later phases use as `cohort_pnrs`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Example B: exposure defined by a hospital diagnosis (ICD-10 codes)</summary>

```r
# Step 2B: identify the exposed via ICD diagnosis ------------------------------
# Same LPR pattern as Phase 9 - but without semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE),
# as the cohort does not yet exist. You query the full population to identify the exposed.
lpr_diag <- read_register("lpr_diag") %>%
  rename_with(tolower)
lpr_adm  <- read_register("lpr_adm") %>%
  rename_with(tolower)

exposed <- lpr_adm %>%
  inner_join(
    lpr_diag %>%
      filter(c_diagtype %in% c("A", "B"),
             substr(c_diag, 2, 4) == "E11") %>%             # T2D: "DE11" → strip D-prefix
      select(recnum, c_diag),
    by = "recnum"
  ) %>%
  select(pnr, index_date = d_inddto) %>%
  collect() %>%
  group_by(pnr) %>%
  arrange(index_date) %>%
  slice(1) %>%                                              # first diagnosis per person
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(exposed = 1L)
```

::: {.callout-note}
This example pulls from LPR2 only. Decide which registers your exposure needs (LPR2, possibly the psychiatric LPR2 tables, and LPR3) and combine them as in [Extract from LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd). If you leave out a register, you miss the cases that only appear there.
:::

</details>

## Step 3 - Exclude prevalent cases {.step-heading}

People who already had your outcome before the index date must be excluded,
otherwise they count as new cases even though they are not. The convention used
throughout this guide: a diagnosis on or before the index date is prevalent
(`<=`), and only one after it is an outcome (`>`). This applies to all designs,
including a prevalence study without a comparison group, so it
belongs here where you build the exposed cohort.

Count how many drop out at each exclusion step, so you can describe the
attrition and later draw a STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) flow diagram (also called a participant or
attrition diagram; see the [STROBE
checklist](https://www.strobe-statement.org/checklists/)). The generic
N-counting template is in [Phase 6](first-extraction.qmd).

### Code: exclude prevalent cases with a function

If the same check is needed more than once (e.g. also on a comparison group
later, see [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd)), wrap the logic in a
function so the two checks do not drift apart. See [Good coding
practice](good-coding-practice.qmd).

```r
# Step 3: exclude prevalent cases ----------------------------------------------
OUTCOME_CODES <- c("S72")   # hip fracture (example study) - ICD-10 for your outcome, adapt

# diagnoses = every contact with an outcome code, for EVERYONE in BEF (not only
# the exposed), so the same table can be reused for the comparison pool later.
# get_lpr_diagnoses() is the helper from Phase 9 (Extract from LPR): define it first.
all_pnrs <- bef %>%                # bef from Step 1 (still lazy)
  distinct(pnr) %>%                # one row per person
  collect() %>%
  pull(pnr)                        # vector with every pnr in BEF

diagnoses <- get_lpr_diagnoses(
  pnr_vector = all_pnrs,           # everyone, not only the exposed
  icd_codes  = OUTCOME_CODES       # only the outcome codes are fetched
)
# Columns: pnr | date_contact | c_diag | c_diagtype | icd3

# We make our OWN function (a reusable block of code). It takes three arguments:
#   diagnoses = your LPR diagnosis extract (columns: pnr, date_contact, icd3)
#   codes     = the ICD codes that define your outcome (here OUTCOME_CODES)
#   cohort    = the group to check, with pnr + index_date
# It returns the pnr that had the outcome ON or BEFORE their own index date.
prior_outcome_pnrs <- function(diagnoses, codes, cohort) {
  diagnoses %>%
    filter(icd3 %in% codes) %>%
    inner_join(cohort %>% select(pnr, index_date), by = "pnr") %>%   # attach each person's index
    filter(date_contact <= index_date) %>%                           # contacts ON or BEFORE index
    # distinct(pnr) alone is only correct if pnr is unique in your cohort. If
    # it is not (e.g. a comparison cohort matched with replacement, so the
    # same pnr has several index_dates), this over-excludes: a diagnosis that
    # predates only ONE of a person's index_dates would drop them from ALL of
    # their occurrences below, not just that one. Fix: distinct(pnr,
    # index_date) here, and anti_join(prevalent, by = c("pnr", "index_date"))
    # in place of the filter(!pnr %in% prevalent) below - same idea as nmi.qmd.
    distinct(pnr) %>%                                                 # one row per person
    pull(pnr)                                                         # vector of pnr's to exclude
}

prevalent <- prior_outcome_pnrs(diagnoses, OUTCOME_CODES, exposed)

n_before <- nrow(exposed)                     # nrow() = number of rows (here: number of persons)
exposed <- exposed %>%
  filter(!pnr %in% prevalent)                 # keep only those WITHOUT a prevalent outcome - see the comment above if pnr repeats

# cat() simply prints a readable line in the console so you can follow the attrition.
cat("After prevalence exclusion:", nrow(exposed),
    "| excluded:", n_before - nrow(exposed), "\n")
# If the message is only for yourself, you can settle for:  nrow(exposed)   # number remaining

stopifnot(n_distinct(exposed$pnr) == nrow(exposed))   # check: one row per person
```

**Planning a comparison cohort?** Extract the outcome (and exposure) dates for
the whole population here rather than just for the exposed, and reuse them:
restricted to the exposed as above, and later for the comparison pool (see
[Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd)). Filtering the diagnosis codes
returns everyone with the diagnosis anyway, so it saves a second query against
the registers.

**If that comparison group is matched with replacement, know what
`distinct(pnr) %>% pull(pnr)` excludes.** `prior_outcome_pnrs()` checks each
row against that row's own `index_date` (the `inner_join` before the filter),
but the final `distinct(pnr)` collapses the result to a plain list of people,
so `filter(!pnr %in% prevalent)` drops every row for that `pnr`, not just the
one where they had a prevalent outcome. If the same person is matched to a different case
with an earlier `index_date`, where they did not yet have the outcome, that
instance gets excluded too. That may be the conservative rule you want, but
decide it on purpose. See [the callout on repeated `pnr` on Comparison
cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd#step-4---assemble-validate-and-save) for the
general repeated-`pnr` problem this is one version of.

## Participant flow diagram (STROBE)

The N counts you made in Step 2 and Step 3 come together in a STROBE flow
diagram: a figure showing how many people were in from the start, how many
were excluded at each step and why, and how many ended up in the study
population. The diagram below also shows where the data comes from at each step (the numbers are
simulated).

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A[("Source registers - whole population<br>LPR2: lpr_sksopr + lpr_adm<br>LPR3: lpr_a_procregistrering + lpr_a_kontakt")]:::store
    B["Step 2: filter on exposure codes<br>exposed with pnr + index_date<br>n = 12,300"]:::step
    E1["Excluded in Step 3:<br>prevalent outcome before index<br>(from LPR diagnoses)<br>n = 1,150"]:::excl
    C["Exposed cohort<br>n = 11,150"]:::step
    F["Optional:<br>+ matched comparison cohort"]:::optional
    D["Final study population<br>pnr + index_date<br>(→ Phase 11)"]:::result

    A --> B
    B --> C
    B -.->|attrition| E1
    C -.-> F
    C --> D
    F -.-> D

    classDef store fill:#eef0f2,stroke:#8a94a6,color:#1f2733;
    classDef step fill:#eaf2fb,stroke:#4a78b5,color:#173a5e;
    classDef excl fill:#fdecea,stroke:#d9534f,color:#7a1f1a;
    classDef optional fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#e69500,color:#7a4f00;
    classDef result fill:#e9f7ef,stroke:#3fae6b,color:#14532d;
```

How each step maps to the data:

- **Source registers:** the whole population's LPR data (you have no cohort list
  yet). LPR2 and LPR3 are opened lazily with `read_register()`, see Step 2
  above.
- **Step 2:** you filter on your exposure codes and attach `pnr` + `index_date`.
  The result is `exposed`.
- **Step 3 (exclusion):** prevalent cases (people with the outcome before their
  index date) are found in the LPR diagnoses and removed. That is the
  `n_before - nrow(exposed)` shown in the exclusion box.
- **Final study population:** `pnr` + `index_date` per person, ready for [Phase
  11 - Extract variables](extract-variables.qmd). If you build a comparison
  cohort, [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd) comes before the last
  step.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Output control:** the exclusion boxes show raw counts. Small numbers (e.g. an
exclusion group with very few people) can be disclosive. What to do about them
before the diagram leaves DST is in [Phase 14 - A hidden number must not be
possible to work out](export.qmd#back-calculation).
:::

## Next step depends on your design {#what-now-choose-your-design}

- **Prevalence study / cohort without a comparison group:** after this page you
  are done: you have your study population with an index date. Continue to
  [Phase 11 - Extract variables](extract-variables.qmd) and [Phase 12 -
  Assemble and prepare the dataset](data-manipulation.qmd).
- **Cohort study with a comparison cohort:** continue to [Comparison
  cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd), where you build a match pool
  and risk-set match a comparison group.
- **(Nested) case-control:** continue to [Case-control](case-control.qmd),
  where your "exposed" group above is instead your cases, and you sample controls who were at risk when the case
  had the outcome.
- **Self-controlled or sibling design:** the person, or the family, is
  their own control - see [Self-controlled and sibling
  designs](special-designs.qmd).
- **Parents, siblings or a parent's characteristics:** see [Family
  links](family-links.qmd) for how to link a child to its parents.

## Further information

- **The Danish Civil Registration System (CPR):** Pedersen CB, Gøtzsche H,
  Møller JØ, Mortensen PB. "[The Danish Civil Registration System. A cohort of
  eight million
  persons](https://content.ugeskriftet.dk/sites/default/files/scientific_article_files/2018-10/dmb3816.pdf)",
  *Dan Med Bull* 2006;53(4):441-9. Documents what CPR contains and how far back
  it reaches: immigrations and emigrations plus municipality of residence from
  1971, Greenland from May 1972, and full address from 1977.
